description: The focus of this cluster is on the problems, efficacy, and dynamics of virtual teams. In his discussion of the shortcomings of conventional teamwork techniques in boosting the performance of virtual teams, Berry (2011) makes the case that particular tactics are required for virtual settings. With an emphasis on managing a virtual workplace, Cascio (2000) provides guidance on how businesses might adjust to virtual work environments. Powell et al. (2004) highlights the growing significance of virtual teams in modern workplaces by offering a thorough analysis of the body of research on the topic and suggesting future study possibilities. Although Warkentin et al. (1997) conduct exploratory research that compares virtual teams with face-to-face teams, stressing the unique benefits and difficulties of virtual communication technologies, Townsend et al. (1998) investigate the technological features and potential future consequences of virtual teams.

This cluster looks at a number of workplace topics, with a special emphasis on COVID-19’s effects, mobile remote presence integration, and dispute resolution. In his exploration of the nuances of conflict in geographically dispersed teams, Hinds and Mortensen (2005) name moderating elements such as shared identity and impromptu communication. In his analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic’s significant effects and ramifications, Kniffin et al. (2021) offer guidance for upcoming workplace investigations and initiatives. In his study of mobile remote presence usage in the workplace, Lee and Takayama (2011) examine social norms and how these technologies alter presence and interpersonal interactions in a virtual work setting.

This cluster focuses on leadership in the context of digital transformation and crisis management. Bartsch et al. (2021) investigate how service staff members might be guided by effective leadership during crisis-driven digital transformations, as the ones brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic. Contreras et al. (2020) examine teleworking and e-leadership both during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, outlining current knowledge and suggesting future lines of inquiry. In his study of the function of leadership in a digitally connected society, Cortellazzo et al. (2019) give a general picture of how digitalisation affects leadership behaviours and the adjustments that must be made by leaders in virtual settings.

This cluster looks on what makes working collaboratively in virtual environments easier. Herbsleb et al. (2002) examine the effects of chat and instant messaging on communication and teamwork since they were introduced in the workplace. Hülsheger et al. (2009) summarise 30 years of research to offer a thorough understanding of what motivates innovation in teams and does a meta-analysis to find team-level predictors of innovation at work. To provide a framework for collaborative working, Patel et al. (2012) identify important elements that support productive collaboration in online settings.

The assessment of virtuality in enterprises and the idea of digital entrepreneurship are the main topics of this cluster. Chudoba et al. (2005) provide measures for evaluating virtuality and looks into the impact of an organisation’s virtuality on worldwide operations. Hull et al. (2007) provide a typology of digital entrepreneurship, examining the various forms of digital entrepreneurship that may be found as well as how digital opportunities can be used for entrepreneurial endeavours.
